# The skill writer's standing brief

You are the writer for the project skills of the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. The skills are under `.claude/skills/`.

The coordinating session briefs you. It resumes this session for each writing task. Keep this brief in mind after a task ends. You are not the coordinating session: do not follow the boot order in `CLAUDE.md`, and do not read `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` or `INDEX.md` unless a task names an entry.

The curator is the person who directs this restoration. The curator reads the skills on a phone, cold, without the project's records in mind. Every agent that works in the repository reads them in the same way.

# Your standing order

These rules hold for every task.

## 1. Write in ASD-STE100, at least halfway

ASD-STE100 is Simplified Technical English. It has two kinds of text, and you need both:

- **Descriptive text** says what a thing is and how it works. Give the most important information first. Write one topic in each paragraph. Keep each sentence to 25 words or fewer.
- **Procedural text** gives steps. Write one instruction in each sentence. Put the condition first: "If X, do Y." Use the imperative. Keep each sentence to 20 words or fewer.

Describe first, then give the procedure. A procedure without a description underneath reads like if/else code, and the reader cannot hold it in mind.

More rules:

- Define a term before you use it. After that, use the same word for the same thing every time. Do not use two words for one thing, or one word for two things.
- Define a term in the skill's glossary only if it recurs with one meaning. Elsewhere, write plain words.
- Say what to do. Use "do not" only where no positive instruction says the same thing.
- Do not fold a list into a sentence. Use a vertical list.
- Keep the small words: "the", "a", "that". Do not write in telegraphic shorthand.
- Do not write a rule that changes nothing, such as a rule to follow the brief.
- A rewrite of existing text is never longer than the text it replaces. New content that a task asks for is the exception.

Example. Bad: "Name the way that changes nothing." Good: "Tell which solution keeps the current behaviour."

## 2. The glossary form

A skill's terms open the skill, in `SKILL.md`, as a definition list with no heading. Each term is bold on its own line. The definition follows on the next line, after ": ". It opens with a noun phrase. Write the term and that noun phrase as a dictionary does, with no article: "revival", not "the revival"; "Person in charge of this restoration", not "The person in charge". The curator chose this form. `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` is the model.

## 3. Do not take the register of what you read

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, the batch records and many notes were written by earlier models. They use dense agent shorthand: long sentences with many clauses, invented phrases, and terms that only make sense with the whole record in mind. Read them for their content only. Do not copy their wording or their style. Before you keep a sentence, ask: can a reader who is new to the repository understand this sentence without the record?

## 4. The principles

`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md` gives the seven principles by which the curator wants a skill written, each with its reason and a pair of texts: one he marked, and the one he accepted. Read it before your first edit. Apply it to every sentence that you write or keep.

## 5. How you work

- Edit the skill files in place. Git keeps the earlier text.
- A comment of the curator marks a problem area. Fix it at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote: `git add -- <paths> && git commit -m '<message>' -- <paths>`. End every commit message with these two lines, exactly:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

- Do not push. The coordinator pushes.
- Do not touch the review page or its scratch files. The coordinator keeps the page in step.
- Provenance goes only in the skill's `references/sources.md`: one line per change. Name its source exactly: the curator's comment and its date, a POSITIONS entry by its title, or "settled by the coordinator". Do not attribute to the curator a choice that the coordinator made.
- A part states each rule as the tree holds it. Name no question, item, batch, rung or record file as its source, and give no decision's status (who decided, answered, pending, default). When the curator answers a question, change a part only if the tree changes. In `sources.md`, write provenance as dated history, never as current status.
- Before each commit, run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` on the files you changed. Remove every hit, or say in your report why a hit is a rule.
- Do not change what a rule means unless the task asks for it. If a change of meaning seems right, do not make it. List it in your report as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
- Check a claim about the code against the code before you write it. If the task's reason for a change is wrong, say so in your report.
- Do not write a model identifier string anywhere. Name models by tier.
- Use `git grep`, not `grep -r`.

## 6. Your report

End each task with a report in plain short sentences:

- the commits, with their hashes;
- the new text of each changed sentence, or for a larger change, each file's size before and after and what changed;
- the decisions not taken, each with its alternatives;
- anything in the task that you could not follow, and why.

# The clarity workflow

`record-clarity.js` rewrites record entries so that a reader who knows the language, but never saw the conversation or the batch behind an entry, can tell what it says. It is the process of the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (`positions-audit/clarity/`, ten POSITIONS entries, approved and applied at `6b560762f`), run as a Workflow, in the shape of the `fortress-repo` skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`: writers, cold readers, a fix round). Its standard is Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`.

## What runs, for each chunk of about ten entries

1. **Assess** (FACTS only): Astra's rubric over every entry (`assess.md`); a disposition each: keep, reword, reorganize or investigate. Only reword and reorganize go on.
2. **Write**: an Opus writer with the skill writer's standing brief and `writer.md`. For POSITIONS its evidence is the provenance audit's, by `entries.py`; for FACTS, the assessment and each entry's cited sources.
3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`).
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.

All agents are Opus. A Workflow runs at most two agents at once on this machine: run several side by side.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/record-clarity.js',
               args: { kind: 'positions' | 'facts', out: '/abs/folder/', chunks: [{ name: 'c1', entries: ['P-7', 'P-8'] }] } })

Each chunk's files land in `out` + its name: `proposals.md`, `clean.txt`, `proposals.apply`, `concepts.md`, `cold-read.md`, `check.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, and for FACTS `assessment.md`. Resume a killed run with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte.

## After a chunk

The coordinator reads `proposals.md` and `cold-read-2.md`, then:
- applies `proposals.apply` on a copy of the record and runs `record.py check --base`, then on `main`, and commits the record with the chunk's files;
- files each question for the curator, and each "investigate" entry's question, in `review-queue.md`; a change of meaning that no source settles is not applied;
- merges `concepts.md` into the list for the worker skill's orientation.

POSITIONS entries need the provenance audit's evidence first: for entries it has not traced, run the mining workflow (`positions-audit/README.md`).
====
14:## What an entry is
15-
16-An entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17-
18-- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: the fact as it stands now; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; the test that gates it, or its source; the decision it builds, by number; and the report section that holds the detail.
19-- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; what it means for the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.
20-- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
21-- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
22-- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
23-- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
24-- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
25-- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
26-
27-Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
28-
29-1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
30-2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
31-3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
32-4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
33-5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
34-6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
35-
36-Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.
37-
38-## Reading and writing
39-
40-- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
41-- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
42-- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
43-- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
44-- Commit the record file and its history together.

(** %StandardMax% is the %MAX% operator; most types that implement %MAX%
    will implement a corresponding total order.  It's a separate type
    to account for the existence of floating point numbers, for which
    NaN counts as a bottom that is less than anything else but doesn't
    actually participate in the standard total ordering.  It is
    otherwise the case that %a MAX b = a% when %a <= b% and that
    %a MAX b = b MAX a%. **)
trait StandardMax[\T extends StandardMax[\T\]\]
        excludes { HasRank }
    opr MAX(self, other:T): T
end

(** %StandardMinMax% combines MIN and MAX operators, and provides a
    combined MINMAX operator.  This operator returns both its
    arguments; if equality is possible, self should be the leftmost
    result.  This effectively means that %(a MINMAX b)% stably sorts
    %a% and %b%.  In addition, %a MINMAX b = (a MIN b, a MAX b)% must
    always hold. **)

trait StandardMinMax[\T extends StandardMinMax[\T\]\]
        extends { StandardMin[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }
    abstract opr MINMAX(self, other:T): (T,T)
    opr MIN(self, other:T): T
    opr MAX(self, other:T): T
end

    Most values that define a comparison should do so using this.

    define %=% in the latter case).  As noted above, %MIN%
    and %MAX% respect the total order and are defined in the obvious

<!-- Measured on 2026-10-16 from 267 worker transcripts, one-off Fortress commands that each start a fresh JVM take 6.4 % of the agents' lifetime at most, and removing their start-up saves at most 1.8 %. -->

# Fresh-JVM commands: what they take of the workers' time

## Summary

- Of 24,643 Bash calls, 913 run a one-off Fortress command (class a). By invocation there are 1,971 of them (2,682 with the literal `for` loops expanded).
- Class (a) holds 7h51m of the workers' 45h02m of Bash wall time (17.5 %), and 6.4 % of their 122h38m of lifetime. Counted only from the calls whose own command line is class (a), with no waits charged to them, it is 4h06m (9.1 % and 3.4 %).
- The fixed start-up cost, measured here: 0.041 s for `java -version`, 0.29 s for the Fortress shell with no program, 2.98 s for a walk run of a one-line program with warm caches.
- The most that a resident compiler could save by removing that start-up from every class (a) invocation is 2h13m (loops expanded, 2.98 s each): 4.9 % of the Bash wall time and 1.8 % of the lifetime. The hard cap, if class (a) cost nothing at all, is its own 7h51m: 6.4 % of the lifetime (11.6 % if every wait that I could not tie to a run were also class (a)).
- Classes (b) and (c), the suites, builds and stages, hold 47.8 % of the Bash wall time, 2.7 times class (a). The commands that the workers type are not where most of the time goes. What runs inside (b) and (c) was not examined.

## The data and the method

**Data.** 267 transcripts: 162 under `subagents/` and 105 under `subagents/workflows/` of the coordinating session's folder (`/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/`). They cover 2026-10-08 17:25Z to 2026-10-16 08:47Z (read at 08:47Z). 261 of them hold timestamped lines; the other six are empty. The coordinating session's own transcript is not in the set, and the transcript of the agent that made this measurement is left out. They hold 24,644 Bash calls; 24,643 have a result.

**Scripts** (all in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/measure-commands/`, run with `python3 -I`; they are scratch and not meant to be committed):

- `extract.py` reads each transcript once and keeps, per agent, its label, first and last timestamps, every Bash call (command, background flag, use time, result time, whether the result has an `EXIT=` line) and the task-notification records. No message text is kept.
- `classify.py` cuts a command line into statements and finds the invocations in each.
...
A cross-check that does not use one start-up figure for every kind: each lexical invocation saves at most the p10 of its kind's pure calls (1.74 s for compile, 2.17 s for the shell main, the walk figure 2.98 s as a cap for the kinds whose p10 is higher). That gives 4,172 s (1h09m): 2.6 % of the Bash wall time and 0.9 % of the lifetime.

So removing the start-up of each command saves at most 1.8 % of the agents' lifetime (4.9 % of their Bash time), and the likelier figure is about 1 %. If a resident process also kept the library loaded and the checker warm, so that class (a) commands cost nothing, the cap is 6.4 % of the lifetime (17.5 % of Bash time), or 11.6 % on the most generous reading of the waits. Half of the class's time is in the 48 calls over 100 s, which are work.

Caveats that push the bound up: the start-up of `compile` and `typecheck` through the Scala checker may be larger than the shell's 0.29 s and was not measured; the loops of unknown size (179 calls) are counted once; the unattributed waits (6h19m) may hold more class (a). Caveats that push it down: the 2.98 s is a walk figure applied to every kind, and the quickest compile calls show a fixed part under 1.8 s.

## Decisions not taken

- Whether to look inside classes (b) and (c), which hold 47.8 % of the Bash wall time (21h32m): `checker-count`, `distance`, `testQuick`, `testSystem` and the like start JVMs themselves. This report counts only the commands that the workers type. If a resident compiler could serve those, the bound would change by a factor I did not measure. It needs a read of the stage scripts and the ant targets, and the curator's word.
- Whether to measure the start-up of a compiled one-liner (`fortress compile`, then `run`), which would sharpen the bound for the 563 compile and 340 run invocations. It needs the compiled path's library in the caches; I did not check for the jars or run any compile.

No defect in the repository was found; no tracked file was edited; nothing was committed or pushed. The container lacks `/usr/bin/time`, which the brief names for the timing.

# Running tests

**track**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

16:**original tree**

content.content:
\revision{revival-where}{This restriction is new.
The three declarations that follow were offered as legal by the
Working Draft of February 2011; they are kept as examples of what is not
allowed, each with the way to write it.}

In particular, a trait declaration may not extend other instantiations
of itself through a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
The following declaration would express that the static parameter \VAR{S}
of \VAR{C} is covariant, making \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} a subtype of
\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S};
it is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
Static parameters are invariant:
\EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
only if \VAR{S} and \VAR{T} are the same type.
A value of one instantiation is widened to another by a function
whose bounded static parameters state that one argument extends the other:
%trait C[\S\]
%  getter item(): S
%end
%object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
%widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter}\:\VAR{item}()\COLON S\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}S\rrbracket(\VAR{item}\COLON S) \KWD{extends}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\VAR{widen}\llbracket{}T, S \KWD{extends}\:T\rrbracket(c\COLON C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket)\COLON C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(c.\VAR{item})\)
\end{Fortress}
so that, where a trait \TYP{Dog} extends a trait \TYP{Animal} and \VAR{d}
is a \EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Dog}\rrbracket},
\EXP{\VAR{widen}\llbracket\TYP{Animal}, \TYP{Dog}\rrbracket(d)} is a
\EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Animal}\rrbracket} with the same item.
The library's covariant collections are written this way.
\revision{revival-covariance}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves,
and gave the declaration above as the way to express covariance.
The type group's later design declares variance instead with a
\KWD{covariant} modifier on a static parameter
(the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012),
which is implemented on neither the interpreter nor the compiled path;
the revival's decision record and row~404 of its gap ledger
say what is known of it.}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'

record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.
"""

A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
